tts: This morning we are talking about one of the hottest new trends in travel — learning holidays. Ilana Canter is senior editor of the travel magazine Escape.

Last autumn I did a falconry course at Ashford Castle in Ireland. It is incredible. You are walking through the grounds of this historic castle, which dates back to 1228, with a huge bird perched on your arm. It feels magical. And no, it is not dangerous at all — the falcons are well trained, so it is very safe.

If you ever wanted to go to space camp as a child but never got the chance, the Adult Space Academy in Alabama runs three-day courses. You are taught how to launch and land a space shuttle, and using flight simulators you experience low gravity and get to have a go at moon-walking. The cost includes accommodation in the space centre, where you share a small room with up to seven people, so you get the full astronaut experience.

And this one is unusual: in Rome there is a gladiator school. You get a chance to experience what it was like to fight as a gladiator. It is a bit like a martial arts workout — hand-to-hand combat with the instructors, and they give you the full Roman outfit. At the end you get a little certificate.

tts: Ashford Castle dates all the way back to 1228. The falcons are well trained, so it is super safe.

The Adult Space Academy is at the US Space and Rocket Centre in Alabama, and it holds three-day courses. You are taught how to launch and land a space shuttle, and you experience the conditions of low gravity.
You share small rooms with up to seven other people, so you really get the full astronaut experience.
The gladiator school is in Rome. The instructors are from the Historic Group of Rome, and at the end you get a little certificate saying that you have completed the course.

tts: You know what I would love to do one day? I would love to go to Peru and walk the Inca Trail — the path that takes you from the Amazon rainforest through the Andes to Machu Picchu.

Ah, I would love to go to Machu Picchu. Apparently the views are absolutely stunning. Not sure about the trek, though. Sounds like hard work — trekking up and down mountains with all your baggage. You would have to be really fit.
That is all part of the challenge.
And then you would have to camp in tents with very basic facilities. It is not really my thing. I am not very good at roughing it. I like life’s little luxuries.
Oh, come on. You need to be more adventurous. Step out of your comfort zone. It is really good for you sometimes.

The second speaker has no interest in Machu Picchu itself.
The second speaker is worried about the physical difficulty.
The second speaker enjoys camping with basic facilities.
The first speaker encourages the second to be more adventurous.

acts.title: Two Englishes, and when the difference matters
rule: American and British English differ in vocabulary far more than in grammar, and at B2 the vocabulary is what will actually cause a misunderstanding. Neither is more correct. What matters is choosing one and not mixing them inside a single piece of writing.
points: This is where most of the difference sits: transport, streets, food and housing.
A few words exist in both varieties with different meanings. In BrE a boot is part of a car; in AmE it is footwear.
-our / -or (colour, color), -re / -er (centre, center), -ise / -ize (both are used in Britain; only -ize in America).
Examiners and editors do not mind which you use. They mind if you use both in the same document.
eg: The luggage space in a car.
And in Britain a subway is a pedestrian tunnel.
acts.careful: “I put the luggage in the boot” is perfectly clear in London and faintly alarming in Chicago. When you are writing for an international reader, choose the word that carries least risk.

write.q: Choose one of the three learning holidays from the interview — falconry, the space academy or the gladiator school — and write about 170 words explaining why you would or would not go. Use the past perfect at least twice when you refer back to earlier experience, and keep your vocabulary consistently British or consistently American throughout.
plan: which one, and why it appeals
what you had done before that is relevant
write.model:
Of the three, the falconry course is the only one I would actually book, and I am slightly surprised by that.

I had never held a bird of any kind until a market in Almaty two years ago, where a man let me hold a hawk for about eight seconds in exchange for a photograph. I had expected it to feel like holding a cat. It felt like holding something that had decided, temporarily, not to leave.

The space academy is not really my thing. I am more of a ground-level person, and sharing a small room with seven strangers is a price I stopped being willing to pay at about twenty-four.

The gladiator school I would enjoy for an hour and regret for a week. By the time I had finished the first session I would have pulled something.

So: Ireland, a castle, and a bird that is only there because it has chosen to be. I would take a return ticket and go out of season.
